title: Why Does Metal Feel Colder Than Wood?
pause_note: long: beats listed in 'long' get a 1.5 s pause

beats: Touch a metal railing and a wooden bench on the same winter morning.
The metal feels freezing. The wood feels almost warm.
But put a thermometer on both, and they read about the same.
So what is your hand actually measuring?
By the end, you'll know why a sauna doesn't burn you,
why a metal slide can, and how mint fools the very same sensors.
Leave anything in a room long enough, and it settles at room temperature.
Metal, wood, plastic, even the air itself.
Nothing in that room is colder than anything else.
Your skin has no thermometer.
It has nerve endings that react to their own temperature, and to how fast it is changing.
One of the main cold sensors is a protein called TRPM8.
When the skin around it cools, it opens, and sends a simple message to your brain: cold.
Your hand is warmer than the room, about thirty-four degrees Celsius at the surface.
So heat flows out of your skin, into whatever you touch.
How fast depends on the material.
Aluminium conducts heat roughly a thousand to two thousand times better than pine wood.
And air conducts about five times worse than pine.
When two things touch, the place where they meet settles at a temperature in between.
It lands closer to the material that moves heat better.
Touch aluminium at twenty degrees, and your skin's surface drops almost to twenty.
Touch pine at twenty degrees, and your skin stays around thirty.
Same object temperature. A very different skin temperature.
And skin temperature is what your cold sensors report.
Now flip it around.
On a hot summer day, a metal slide in full sun can get hot enough to burn skin.
A wooden bench in the same sun feels warm, but rarely dangerous.
Same physics, reversed.
The metal pours its heat into your skin. The wood can't deliver it fast enough.
That's also how a hot sauna works.
The air is often eighty to a hundred degrees Celsius, and yet people sit in it for minutes.
Air is a poor conductor, and it holds very little heat, so it delivers heat to your skin slowly.
The benches are wood, for the same reason.
But touch a bare metal nail in that bench, and it can burn you.
Your cold sensors can even be fooled with no heat flowing at all.
Menthol, the cool part of mint, sticks to TRPM8 and makes it open even at warm skin temperature.
The sensor fires, and your brain hears: cold.
Nothing actually got colder.
So your hand is not a thermometer.
It reports what is happening to your own skin: how far it cools, and how fast.
Metal is not colder than wood. It just pulls your heat away faster.
Next time you grab a cold railing, remember: you're not feeling the cold. You're feeling your own heat, leaving.
Which surface in your home feels the coldest? Tell me in the comments.
